country.name: United Kingdom
country.tagline: Chalk, climate change and Champagne grapes: the country that invented the idea of sparkling wine is now making it seriously.

stats.note: WineGB Industry Report 2025: 4,841 ha, 1,104 vineyards, 238 wineries, about 10.6 million bottles from the 2024 harvest (about 0.08 mhl), 69 percent sparkling. A larger 2025 harvest was widely reported in March 2026.

country.overview:
Britain has drunk wine since the Romans, but for most of history it bought rather than made it: claret from Bordeaux, sherry, port and Champagne were all, in part, English commercial creations. Its own vineyards are a modern phenomenon. About 4,840 hectares are now planted, mostly in the south-east of England, and the area has more than doubled in ten years. Kent has the most vines, followed by West Sussex, Essex, East Sussex and Hampshire.

The reason is sparkling wine. The chalk that runs from Champagne under the Channel and resurfaces in the North and South Downs, combined with a cool climate that has warmed enough to ripen Chardonnay, Pinot Noir and Pinot Meunier most years, gives base wines with the high acidity that traditional-method sparkling needs. Nyetimber, planted in West Sussex in 1988, and Ridgeview, planted in 1995, proved the point, and English sparkling wines now beat Champagne in blind tastings and international competitions. About 69 percent of production is sparkling and nearly all of it is made by the traditional method. Champagne houses have invested too: Taittinger at Domaine Evremond in Kent and Pommery in Hampshire.

Still wine is the other half of the story. Bacchus, a German crossing, gives elderflower-scented whites that have become England's answer to Sauvignon Blanc, and riper vintages have produced convincing Pinot Noir and Chardonnay. Essex's Crouch Valley, one of the driest places in Britain, is now a source of fine still Pinot. Weather remains the risk: spring frost, wet flowering and cool autumns can halve a crop, as in 2024, while 2018 and 2025 were large.

Legally, the UK has four wine PDOs: English Wine and Welsh Wine (both registered with the EU in 2011 and carried into UK law after Brexit), Darnibole (a single Cornish Bacchus vineyard, 2017) and Sussex (2022), the first regional PDO for sparkling wine.

history.title: Roman vineyards
history.text: Excavations at Wollaston in the Nene valley, Northamptonshire, revealed planting trenches of a Roman vineyard covering several hectares, the largest evidence of Roman viticulture in Britain.

history.title: Domesday vineyards
history.text: The Domesday Book records more than 40 vineyards, many attached to monasteries and producing communion wine.

history.title: Bordeaux becomes English
history.text: Eleanor of Aquitaine's marriage to Henry Plantagenet brought Bordeaux under the English crown for three centuries, and claret became England's wine.

history.title: Christopher Merret's paper
history.text: Merret presented 'Some Observations concerning the Ordering of Wines' to the Royal Society, describing how coopers added sugar and molasses to make wine 'brisk and sparkling', decades before Champagne made sparkling wine deliberately. Strong English coal-fired glass made it possible.

history.title: Painshill's vineyard
history.text: Charles Hamilton planted a vineyard at Painshill in Surrey whose sparkling wine was reportedly passed off as Champagne; it has been replanted.

history.title: Hambledon
history.text: Major-General Sir Guy Salisbury-Jones planted Hambledon in Hampshire, generally counted as the first commercial vineyard of the modern English revival.

history.title: Nyetimber
history.text: Stuart and Sandy Moss planted Champagne varieties at Nyetimber in West Sussex; the first wine, a 1992 Blanc de Blancs, launched English sparkling wine.

history.title: PDOs
history.text: English and Welsh wine were registered as PDOs in 2011, Darnibole in 2017 and Sussex in July 2022.

country.classification: Four PDOs: English Wine and Welsh Wine (grapes 100 percent from England or Wales, vineyards below 220 m, quality sparkling limited to Chardonnay, Pinot Noir, Pinot Meunier, Pinot Noir Précoce, Pinot Blanc and Pinot Gris), Darnibole (Bacchus from a single Cornish valley) and Sussex (2022, the first regional PDO, with at least 15 months on lees for sparkling). Two PGIs, English Regional Wine and Welsh Regional Wine, allow hybrids such as Seyval Blanc. WineGB's 'Great British Classic Method' hallmark covers traditional-method PDO wines.
country.climate_soils: A cool maritime climate, warmed by the Gulf Stream, with long, mild growing seasons in good years. The best sites are south-facing slopes on chalk (North and South Downs, Hampshire, Kent), greensand and clay (the Weald), with drier, warmer conditions in Essex and East Anglia. Frost, rain at flowering and autumn rot are the main risks.

grapes.name: Chardonnay
grapes.note: The most planted grape; backbone of sparkling and increasingly fine still wine.

grapes.name: Pinot Noir
grapes.note: Sparkling and, in warm years, still red.

grapes.name: Bacchus
grapes.note: The aromatic still-wine signature, elderflower and nettle.

grapes.name: Seyval Blanc
grapes.note: A hardy hybrid of the early revival, still used for sparkling.

regions.name: South East England
regions.tagline: Kent, Sussex and Surrey: chalk downs and the heart of English sparkling wine.
regions.summary: Kent (the largest planted county), West and East Sussex and Surrey hold most of the UK's vineyards. The North and South Downs are chalk, the Weald between them clay and greensand. Nyetimber, Ridgeview, Rathfinny, Wiston, Bolney, Chapel Down, Gusbourne, Hush Heath, Domaine Evremond (Taittinger) and Denbies are here. Sussex gained its own PDO in 2022.
regions.history: Kent and Sussex had medieval monastic vineyards; Bolney (1972) and Breaky Bottom (1974) were early modern pioneers, and Nyetimber (1988) and Ridgeview (1995) proved that Champagne varieties could make world-class sparkling wine here. Champagne houses followed: Taittinger planted Domaine Evremond in Kent from 2017.
regions.terroir: Chalk of the North and South Downs, Wealden clay and greensand between them; maritime climate, warm summers close to the Channel.
regions.grapes: Chardonnay, Pinot Noir, Pinot Meunier, Bacchus, Seyval Blanc, Solaris and others
regions.styles: Traditional-method sparkling (most of the output), still white, rosé and some red
regions.classification: PDO English Wine (or Welsh Wine in Wales) and the English/Welsh Regional Wine PGIs; Sussex PDO (2022)

regions.name: Wessex
regions.tagline: Hampshire's chalk and the cradle of the modern revival at Hambledon.
regions.summary: Hampshire, Dorset and Wiltshire share chalk downland similar to Champagne. Hambledon (1952) began the modern revival; Hattingley Valley, Exton Park, Coates and Seely and Louis Pommery England are leading names.
regions.history: Hambledon's planting in 1952 began the English revival, and Hampshire's chalk drew investment in the 2000s from Hattingley Valley, Exton Park and the Pommery partnership.
regions.terroir: Chalk downland with flint, similar to Champagne; slightly cooler and higher than Sussex.
regions.grapes: Chardonnay, Pinot Noir, Pinot Meunier, Bacchus, Seyval Blanc, Solaris and others
regions.styles: Traditional-method sparkling (most of the output), still white, rosé and some red
regions.classification: PDO English Wine (or Welsh Wine in Wales) and the English/Welsh Regional Wine PGIs

regions.name: East Anglia
regions.tagline: Dry, sunny Essex and the rise of still English Pinot Noir.
regions.summary: Essex is now the third county by planted area, and the Crouch Valley near Burnham-on-Crouch, one of the driest parts of Britain on London clay, supplies fruit for some of the best still Pinot Noir and Chardonnay, including for Gusbourne and other wineries.
regions.history: Essex and Suffolk had monastic vineyards in the Middle Ages; the modern Crouch Valley plantings date mostly from the 1990s on and expanded fast after 2015.
regions.terroir: London clay and gravels in Essex, one of the driest and sunniest parts of Britain.
regions.grapes: Chardonnay, Pinot Noir, Pinot Meunier, Bacchus, Seyval Blanc, Solaris and others
regions.styles: Traditional-method sparkling (most of the output), still white, rosé and some red
regions.classification: PDO English Wine (or Welsh Wine in Wales) and the English/Welsh Regional Wine PGIs

regions.name: South West England
regions.tagline: Cornish valleys, Devon slate and the Darnibole PDO.
regions.summary: Cornwall, Devon, Somerset and Gloucestershire have smaller, often tourist-led vineyards. Camel Valley in Cornwall, founded by Bob and Annie Lindo in 1989, won international awards for sparkling wine and created the Darnibole PDO for its Bacchus.
regions.history: Roman and medieval vineyards existed in the west country; Camel Valley (1989) is the best-known modern estate.
regions.terroir: Slate, sandstone and clay; mild, wet and windy, so sheltered valleys matter.
regions.grapes: Chardonnay, Pinot Noir, Pinot Meunier, Bacchus, Seyval Blanc, Solaris and others
regions.styles: Traditional-method sparkling (most of the output), still white, rosé and some red
regions.classification: PDO English Wine (or Welsh Wine in Wales) and the English/Welsh Regional Wine PGIs; Darnibole PDO (2017)

regions.name: Wales
regions.tagline: A small but fast-growing wine country with its own PDO.
regions.summary: Wales has about 91 hectares of vines, mostly in the south-east (Monmouthshire, the Vale of Glamorgan) and along the border. Ancre Hill, a biodynamic estate near Monmouth, and Llanerch are the best known. Welsh Wine has been a PDO since 2011.
regions.history: Vines were grown at Castell Coch for the Marquess of Bute in the 1870s; the modern Welsh wine revival dates from the 1970s and accelerated in the 2010s.
regions.terroir: Old red sandstone, limestone and clay; wetter and cooler than south-east England.
regions.grapes: Chardonnay, Pinot Noir, Pinot Meunier, Bacchus, Seyval Blanc, Solaris and others
regions.styles: Traditional-method sparkling (most of the output), still white, rosé and some red
regions.classification: PDO English Wine (or Welsh Wine in Wales) and the English/Welsh Regional Wine PGIs

gb-darnibole.name: Darnibole
gb-darnibole.summary: Darnibole is a single valley-side vineyard of Camel Valley, near Bodmin in Cornwall, registered as a PDO in 2017 for still Bacchus. The rules cap yields at 56 hl/ha and require Bacchus grown on the site's slate soils. It was Britain's first single-vineyard PDO and a statement that English still wine could express place.
gb-darnibole.terroir: Slate soils on a sheltered, south-facing slope above the River Camel.
gb-darnibole.nerd_note: The name is the old Cornish field name for the site.

gb-english-wine.name: English Wine
gb-english-wine.grapes: Chardonnay, Pinot Noir, Pinot Meunier, Pinot Noir Précoce, Pinot Blanc, Pinot Gris for sparkling; many vinifera varieties for still wine
gb-english-wine.summary: The English Wine PDO covers wine made entirely from grapes grown in England in vineyards no higher than 220 metres, with a maximum yield of 80 hl/ha. Quality sparkling wine may come only from the six Champagne and Burgundy grapes, and still wine from a long list of vinifera varieties but not hybrids (which must use the English Regional Wine PGI). Most of England's best wine carries this label, from Nyetimber and Ridgeview to Chapel Down's Bacchus.
gb-english-wine.terroir: Chalk downs, Wealden clay and greensand, Essex clay, Devon and Cornish slate; cool maritime climate.
gb-english-wine.nerd_note: About 91 percent of UK sparkling wine in 2024 was made by the traditional method.

gb-sussex.name: Sussex
gb-sussex.grapes: Chardonnay, Pinot Noir, Pinot Meunier and other classic varieties
gb-sussex.summary: Sussex became the UK's first regional PDO in July 2022 after a campaign by producers including Ridgeview, Wiston, Rathfinny and Bolney. It covers East and West Sussex, with about 1,130 hectares of vines, and sets stricter rules than the English Wine PDO, including at least 15 months on the lees for sparkling wine. The South Downs chalk ridge, Wealden greensand and clay give the county a range of sites, from Rathfinny's chalk bowl near the sea to Nyetimber's greensand at West Chiltington.
gb-sussex.terroir: Chalk of the South Downs, greensand and Wealden clay; maritime climate close to the Channel.
gb-sussex.nerd_note: Breaky Bottom, in a fold of the Downs near Lewes, has made sparkling Seyval Blanc since the 1970s, one of the oldest wineries in Sussex.

gb-welsh-wine.name: Welsh Wine
gb-welsh-wine.grapes: Vinifera varieties; classic varieties for sparkling
gb-welsh-wine.summary: The Welsh Wine PDO mirrors the English rules for grapes grown entirely in Wales. With about 91 hectares in 2025, Wales is small but growing, with vineyards mainly in Monmouthshire and the Vale of Glamorgan.
gb-welsh-wine.terroir: Varied soils on sheltered slopes in south-east Wales; wetter and cooler than south-east England.
gb-welsh-wine.nerd_note: Ancre Hill's sparkling wine won a top award at an international sparkling-wine competition in Italy in 2012, a breakthrough for Welsh wine.

sites.name: Nyetimber
sites.text: The estate at West Chiltington where Stuart and Sandy Moss planted Champagne grapes in 1988; owned since 2006 by Eric Heerema and made by Cherie Spriggs, it now farms about 425 ha across Sussex, Hampshire and Kent and won the IWC Champion Sparkling Wine trophy in 2025.

sites.name: Ridgeview
sites.text: Founded by Mike and Christine Roberts at Ditchling Common in 1995, Ridgeview made only sparkling wine from the start and led the campaign for the Sussex PDO.

sites.name: Rathfinny Wine Estate
sites.text: A large chalk-downland estate near Alfriston, planted from 2012 by Mark and Sarah Driver, three miles from the sea.

sites.name: Wiston Estate
sites.text: The Goring family's estate below Chanctonbury Ring on the South Downs chalk, planted in 2006; its early vintages were made by Dermot Sugrue. Coordinates mark Wiston parish.

sites.name: Bolney Wine Estate
sites.text: One of the oldest Sussex vineyards, planted in 1972 at Bolney in the Weald, known for still Pinot Noir as well as sparkling.

sites.name: Breaky Bottom
sites.text: Peter Hall's tiny vineyard in a fold of the South Downs near Rodmell, planted in 1974 and famous for sparkling Seyval Blanc.

sites.name: Gusbourne
sites.text: An estate at Appledore in Kent, on the edge of Romney Marsh, planted in 2004, known for vintage sparkling and still Pinot Noir and Chardonnay.

sites.name: Chapel Down
sites.text: England's largest wine brand, at Small Hythe near Tenterden, famous for Bacchus and sparkling wine.

sites.name: Hambledon Vineyard
sites.text: Planted by Sir Guy Salisbury-Jones in 1952 on Hampshire chalk and revived from 1999 by Ian Kellett, who made it a traditional-method sparkling estate.

sites.name: Hattingley Valley
sites.text: A Hampshire chalk estate near Medstead and Lower Wield, founded in 2008 and known for a winery that makes wine for many smaller growers.

sites.name: Camel Valley
sites.text: Bob and Annie Lindo's Cornish vineyard, founded in 1989 and now run by their son Sam, with award-winning sparkling wine and the Darnibole Bacchus PDO.

sites.name: Denbies Wine Estate
sites.text: One of the largest single vineyards in England, on the North Downs chalk near Dorking, planted in 1986.

sites.name: Painshill Park vineyard
sites.text: Charles Hamilton's 1740s landscape garden in Surrey included a vineyard whose sparkling wine was said to be sold as Champagne; it has been replanted.

sites.name: Wollaston Roman vineyard
sites.text: Excavations in the Nene valley near Wollaston found trenches for a Roman vineyard covering several hectares, the best evidence of Roman wine-growing in Britain.

sites.name: Ancre Hill
sites.text: A biodynamic estate near Monmouth, Wales' best-known vineyard, making sparkling and still wines.
